articles.title: Whither terrorism
articles.content: THE future of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa remains unclear, whether it’s as a single entity or as a democratic one. PTI, we are told, has been made PNG — once again. And the south of KP is reportedly being carved out rapidly to be a new province or to simply reverse theamendmentthat made the former Fata part of KP. No one is really sure what the coming days hold. Amid this confusion, a newly appointed member of the Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC) for the special emergency-hit districts of the south has created another storm in a teacup. In a video statement he spoke of reaching out to the Afghan Taliban to bring peace to Pakistan. Considering that this preference for dialogue over conflict with the fitna-across-the-border ostensibly has been the reason the PTI government was sent home, a similar message of love from the new advisory council just wasn’t cricket. But before we could get our breath back at this audacity, the new spokesman of the region, Mehmood Jan Babar, added to the mess by not denying the idea altogether. Eventually Samar Bilour, who represents the Peshawar-led advisory council, had to enter the fray to diss the notion of talks. As an aside, we now have a Peshawar council and a Southern council. Be that as it may, the point is these statements have simply added to the confusion surrounding the province. And terrorism, despite the frequency of the attacks and the statements of the government, has taken a backseat. The focus is more on what the grand plan for KP is. Is it simply to close the doors on PTI? Is it to conduct an experiment on the efficacy of newer, smaller provinces? Or is it simply to reverse the Fata merger? Or perhaps it was to give the governor the chance to clear encroachments, a favourite problem for most non-elected officials these days. As the Urdu saying goes, there are as many rumours as there are mouths. We appear to be using the same old playbook put together in the post-Musharraf period. But none of these rumours seem to be highlighting the basic issue — how to address the decades-old problem of militancy in these regions. Other than vague promises of fighting the problem, there is little that has been shared with the people to explain what the new government is doing or planning to do. Militancy is going from bad to worse. The intensity of the attacks is worrying and impacts the entire country, especially one looking for more foreign investment. But while the state is clear on its decision to fight its way to victory, it doesn’t seem to have a clear strategy or path for this — or so it appears to those on the outside. Any strategy to succeed must take into account the current environment. However, we appear to be using the same old playbook put together in the post-Musharraf period when the TTP was controlling large swathes of land in what is now former Fata. In order to flush the Taliban out, military operations were conducted after the ordinary residents were persuaded to leave their homes and villages before the clearing out was done. And once the area/s were cleared, the displaced people were allowed to return to their homes and businesses. However, nearly two decades later, the TTP is no longer controlling areas; it seems to appear only to conduct attacks or block roads, or carry out other activities and then melt away. And yet, it seems, our strategy remains the same — of wanting to clear out areas, be it at the level of villages and so on. But if the TTP is not controlling these areas and the plan is to clear out the residents before launching operations, surely the TTP will also vacate the areas along with the residents and simply return later. How is this effective? And this is all the more difficult now because 20 years earlier, the TTP escaped to an Afghanistan run by a hostile government, which is no longer the case. But these questions are really not being discussed. The intelligence-based operations (IBOs) are also offered as an alternative. Though once again, there is little clarity on how effective these are; they only become public when they lead to deaths of troops, which is tragic. But once again, there is little information available on why there is even one fatality during an IBO. And if they are effective, then why has the problem simply grown? The second problem with this strategy is the public sentiment, which is against military operations because of the displacement and suffering that comes in the wake of this. But more than that, the displacements were not accompanied by the compensation the people had been promised — for the damage to their property and business. This has been a major reason for their reluctance to support operations this time around. And yet, this also does not seem to have led to any kind of brainstorming about what to do differently. More worrying still is the distrust or alienation of the people in general from the state as well as the TTP. In many anecdotal accounts, it is suggested the local residents of the affected areas see the activities of the TTP and the state as alienating. These gaps with the state, ideally, should be bridged before operations are launched. It is rather obvious that kinetic operations cannot succeed without the people’s support. And yet the state seems to be doing little to earn this support or trust. And along with all this comes the larger issue of why the kinetic operations, whenever they have succeeded, are not followed by a successful handover to strong functioning civilian institutions which can then govern effectively. In other words, the build-and-transfer part has eluded us for decades. Indeed, the reduction of the debate over terrorism to a simple one of using force or not is a very one-dimensional one. The problem requires a lot more depth and nuance than is realised.
articles.author: Arifa Noor

articles.title: In a pickle in Jamnagar
articles.content: THE massive Reliance refinery in Jamnagar abutting the Arabian Sea from its perch in Gujarat was inaugurated in December 1999. There may be absolutely no connection between the refinery’s birthday and India’s nuclear tests of May 1998. But it’s difficult also to ignore the high stakes involved in its presence facing Pakistan, which too became a nuclear power that year. History shows a pattern of power play associated with such critical and strategic assets. It was on the eve of World War I that Churchill decided that the Royal Navy should switch to oil and away from Welsh coal to make the fleet faster and more efficient. But with no oil of its own, Britain turned to the Abadan refinery, which would eventually become the world’s largest such facility, except that it was needlessly close to the border with Iraq. The refinery was at the heart of the 1953 coup against Mohammad Mossadegh when the elected prime minister nationalised the oil industry. It was the first scalp for Saddam Hussein in the long war he launched against Iran in 1980. The Jamnagar refinery is said to be the world’s largest facility to process the most difficult of crude oils, including hugely discounted volumes imported from cash-strapped Venezuela. Given its proximity to Pakistan, the facility has figured in comments by analysts and voluble generals alike as a potential target, a veritable sitting duck. The Ambani family on its part has played an active role in seeking to improve ties with Pakistan. They reportedly played a role in pleading through a former US president close to the family in pressing Gen Pervez Musharraf to allow Nawaz Sharif to be able to leave Pakistan to live in exile. The refinery has also featured as a potential bridge between the implacable rivals, at one point offering to transport refined products to Pakistan through the Punjab border. Given the fact that India has only suspended thewarit launched against Pakistan under the sobriquet of Operation Sindoor and not brought it to a closure, the tense ties are expected to continue to keep a range of targets in the crosshairs of both sides. In the prevailing circumstances of a global economic meltdown mocking the poor and the rich alike, it’s probably just a question of a nudge that the proverbial ice is broken between the two, and last week may have offered a sliver of such a hope. The day US Secretary of State Marco Rubio came to visit the Reliance oil refinery in Jamnagar, President Mohamed Muizzu of the Maldives waslanding in Islamabadwhere he would give an unusual call to revive the frozen South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (Saarc). Muizzu’s call had a strange ring to it given that he was elected to lead his archipelago nation in 2023 on the openly anti-India slogan of “India out”. The US wants to dry up Moscow’s wartime oil revenues by pushing India toward alternative heavy crude markets. Seen as close to Beijing and pointedly hostile to New Delhi at the time, Muizzu preferred a mellow approach in Pakistan when Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif broached the two issues he routinely raises: Kashmir and Indus water sharing with India. Leading the first Maldivian state visit to Islamabad in 11 years, Muizzu kept his sights on sweeping maritime security and defence pacts. For both Pakistan and the Maldives, a stronger bilateral relationship is seen as serving as a necessary strategic counterweight to balance India’s regional dominance. Rubio’s visitto Jamnagar was not only aimed at sending more stolen oil from Venezuela for refining with a view to easing the enormous pressure put by the reckless Israel-US war on Iran on global fuel markets. Rubio’s primary objective apparently was to convince Reliance to buy more Venezuelan crude while aggressively cutting its intake of Russian oil. Following Western sanctions on Russia, India became Russia’s top oil buyer. The US wants to dry up Moscow’s wartime oil revenues by pushing India toward alternative heavy crude markets. Gleaning from Rubio’s description, the US sees Jamnagar as the only facility globally with the sheer muscle to offset Russian volumes. Before the visit ended, however, unflattering news came trickling in from Arunachal Pradesh, an Indian-ruled province China claims as South Tibet. The paramilitary patrol keeping vigil for India had had recent face-offs with Chinese counterparts at several parts of the border where they had held their ground valiantly. Or so claimed the paramilitary chief Shatrujeet Kapur. His comments were said to have been taken down and the government denied anything at all was really amiss. Only a couple of days or so before the reported transgressions around Arunachal Pradesh and their denial by New Delhi, the two countries had gone through a notably high-decibel exchange over the naming of geographical features in Ladakh.The Global Times, considered close to China’s ruling Communist Party, wrote a long editorial reminding India of the need to avoid disturbing the agreement on peace and tranquillity along their border. A bird’s-eye view of the South Asia chessboard, therefore, reveals a fraught cross-section of forces at play. Pakistan appears agreeable in its ties with the three big powers — the US, China and Russia. Whereas India has struggled to keep the US in good humour, which makes it even more of an ordeal to avoid annoying Russia, a traditional ally in countless ways. With China, the relations require a greater quotient of tender care but with scant quantities in sight. Add to the mix the Indian youth mobilisation that’s rocked the over 12-year-old government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Has Rubio created more trouble for Modi, including by not even meeting him during the visit, or has he by visiting Jamnagar set the grounds for a diplomatic entente with neighbours? Which would leave Modi elbowroom to address the domestic crisis with any degree of composure or hope to endure the pickle he is in. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.
articles.author: Jawed Naqvi

articles.title: Pakistan for all
articles.content: WHY haven’t we built a Pakistan where everyone enjoys equal rights? Postcolonial rulers in diverse countries had to build four basic pillars at once: capable states, dynamic economies, cohesive nations, and inclusive politics. Diversity, and in many cases inequalities and conflicts, made the last two vital so that diversity doesn’t mean divides. But many ignored these subtle tasks to focus on the state and economy, only to make both non-inclusive. This led to conflicts that damaged states and economies. We did the same and faced the same fate. How can we now reverse gears? The answer is simple: ensure inclusive politics to produce a cohesive nation, which can create a capable state that can shape a dynamic economy, with each feeding the others in a virtuous circle. Are we creating this virtuous circle via inclusion or choking it via exclusion? Inclusive politics needs a political culture where losers can bear losing electorally, knowing they will survive politically to aim for power again. But we have winner-takes-all, zero-sum politics rather than win-win politics — especially in the last four years as the PTI and nationalist parties in KP, Balochistan, and, more recently, Azad Kashmir face not just electoral defeat but also political extinction due to debatable judicial, electoral, and administrative manoeuvres. They are not seen as political rivals to defeat but existential enemies to eliminate. The imposition of emergency rule in KP is the latest such ploy. Credible elections ensure broad ownership and support for tough decisions. Most of our elections have been controversial. The 2024 elections, in particular, are seen by many credible local and global analysts as having been blatantly rigged. Those elected freely must also be empowered fully once in power. In our case, informal power has long been wielded without accountability. But rarely have elected officials looked as clueless as today. The link between power and accountability to the public stands broken. Inclusive politics produces a cohesive nation. While opposing the unconstitutional usurpation of the powers of elected setups, inclusive politics also ensures constitutional checks and balances so that they don’t abuse power. This is done via the horizontal division of power across the executive, parliament, the judiciary, and electoral and accountability state bodies. While such division has always been weak in Pakistan, the boundaries among them have become so blurred in the last four years that the three main power organs look to some like a triumvirate. Inclusive politics also divides power vertically among federal, provincial, and local setups. Such distribution gives different groups a chance to govern. Those who could not win federally in a given election or can never win there due to their limited support still have a chance to win power provincially or locally. It also brings rulers closer to people to make them more accountable. Concentrating power federally turns too many citizens into permanent losers and reduces accountability. But local bodies elections have not been held for long in most provinces and regions, and provinces have usurped the financial and administrative powers of even those in place. Provinces, in turn, face the same fate at the hands of the centre and some see plans to weaken them further by creating small provinces. Inclusive politics also empowers individuals and civic groups to criticise elected setups by giving them a wide range of freedoms and rights. But they have been severely curtailed. HRCP’s last annual report describes growing curbs on free speech and human rights. Journalists, political workers, lawyers, and activists face flimsy cases under draconian cybercrime, sedition, and antiterrorism laws. Threats and disappearances make speaking out dangerous. Instead of reversing gears, we are actually accelerating on the current self-destructive path. The dream of a Pakistan for everyone has given way to a grim reality of a country for a handful of people who monopolise power and wealth. Rulers are gaining power but losing legitimacy and trust. Exclusion rather than inclusion, and coercion rather than consent prevail. The state is struggling to end the violence its past policies helped create, while its current policies risk fuelling violence. A secure state can’t emerge from a divided nation, nor can an economy thrive on exclusion. The inclusionary pillars we neglect will keep weakening the exclusionary pillars we build. With inclusive politics nowhere in sight, a cohesive nation, a capable state and a dynamic economy will remain a pipe dream. The writer has a PhD degree in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and 25 years of grassroots to senior-level experience across 50 countries.
articles.author: Dr Niaz Murtaza

articles.title: Trapped abroad
articles.content: FARID left his home in Narowal in search of a better future. A local agent charged him Rs800,000, promising him a well-paid job abroad. What awaited him, however, was nothing he could have imagined. For two years, he says, he was held in a prison-like compound near the Cambodia-Laos border. His passport had been confiscated, his movements were restricted, and his dreams shattered. Farid’s job was to cook for hundreds of people who, like him, had been trafficked and trapped in scam centres. His working day began at 9am and continued until 4am, leaving him barely a few hours to rest. Any defiance was met with torture, including electric shocks. When authorities launched a crackdown on the scam centre, Farid managed to escape. But his freedom was short-lived as he was apprehended by Cambodian police and remains in a detention centre, waiting to return home. Despite attempts to seek assistance through Pakistani diplomatic channels, Farid struggled to secure support. He approached the National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) for help, but twice his return was held up by documentation requirements. Farid’s story is not unique. In May 2026, the government informed the National Assembly of approximately 15,000 Pakistanis reportedly caught up in fraudulent employment schemes or in camps across Southeast Asia. As authorities have begun cracking down on these operations, thousands of Pakistanis now face difficulties returning home. Some need emergency travel documents, while others face penalties and bureaucratic delays. The same parents who struggled to finance their children’s journey abroad are now having to raise more money to bring them home. We need to look more closely at recruitment networks. Part of the difficulty is that those who have been trafficked are not always recognised as victims. Young people recruited in one country and forced to commit online fraud in another may themselves face arrest when these operations are raided. Their expired visas or confiscated passports become grounds for detention, while the deception and abuse they have suffered receive far less attention. Worse still, confiscated passports and identity documents may be misused by criminal networks to commit further fraud, potentially implicating victims in crimes they never committed. Even after escaping their traffickers, they stay behind bars, while those who exploited them often remain beyond the reach of the law. Across its 2025 and 2026 investigations, Amnesty International identified nearly 100 scam compounds in Southeast Asia, documenting human trafficking, forced labour and torture. As authorities have begun raiding these operations, there are worrying signs that similar criminal networks are now taking root in other parts of the world, including Pakistan. In August 2026, a raid on a suspected illegal call centre in Islamabad resulted in the detention of 500 foreign nationals, including Chinese and Vietnamese citizens. During a visit to Adiala Jail, we met approximately 70 women detained in connection with fraudulent activities. Were they knowingly involved in fraud, or had some been deceived or coerced into working there? Online fraud is a serious crime and those responsible must be held accountable. But enforcement must distinguish between those who organise and profit from these operations and those who may themselves be victims of exploitation. Pakistan already has institutions responsible for different aspects of call-centre operations. Yet many of them operate without registration, and there is insufficient monitoring to ensure that these establishments comply with the law. A regularly updated registry, coupled with effective oversight, would help authorities distinguish between legitimate businesses and unregistered operations. We also need to look more closely at the recruitment networks operating within Pakistan. Who is offering these jobs? Who receives payment? And what action is taken when families report that someone has been trafficked abroad? There must be closer coordination between cybercrime investigators, immigration authorities, anti-trafficking agencies and Pakistan’s diplomatic missions. Foreign nationals arrested in suspected scam operations should be screened for possible trafficking and provided with legal assistance. Pakistanis stranded abroad must have access to timely documentation and repatriation, including in countries without a resident embassy. These are basic responsibilities of a government towards its citizens and towards people who may have been trafficked into its territory. Farid is still waiting in Cambodia, having survived an experience no one should have to endure. It should not be so difficult to bring him home. The writer is the chairperson of the National Commission for Human Rights.
articles.author: Rabiya Javeri Agha

articles.title: Privatisation framework
articles.content: THEproposed mergerof the Privatisation Commission and the Public-Private Partnership Authority (P3A) into a single institution is a sensible move. It will end the duality of functions and provide a more coherent framework for mobilising private capital to manage public assets and develop physical infrastructure for which the state has limited resources to spare. Although the two bodies operate under separate laws, their mandates intersect in bringing private capital and expertise into areas dominated by the state. A unified entity could offer a common platform for evaluating these options. Privatisation involves transferring ownership or control of state assets, while public-private partnerships (PPPs) allow governments to enlist private capital for projects they cannot finance. Both approaches require sound financial assessments and clear risk allocations. With Pakistan facing persistent fiscal constraints, the state cannot afford to finance loss-making enterprises indefinitely. Private investment can help ease these pressures, but it is not an end in itself. Poorly structured transactions can leave the state with inadequate returns or costly contractual obligations. The proposed legislation envisages four public funds to support privatisation and PPP transactions. These instruments could help prepare viable projects and attract investment. However, they must not become vehicles for subsidising commercially unsound ventures. Government guarantees and liabilities should be disclosed and assessed before deals are approved. The proposed legal protections for serving and former officials acting in good faith also require careful rethinking. Officials should be protected against frivolous litigation when making decisions in the public interest. Such protection must not, however, become immunity from accountability. Making PPP agreements accessible as public documents is also positive. Public scrutiny is particularly important when private investors enter long-term arrangements that may impose financial obligations on taxpayers and successive governments. The new arrangement offers an opportunity to improve the management of state assets and infrastructure investment. Its success will depend on securing fair value for public property, attracting credible investors and ensuring that partnerships deliver tangible benefits. The bill proposes a majority-independent board with private-sector representation to strengthen commercial decision-making. Its effectiveness will require transparent appointments, relevant expertise, political independence, clear performance benchmarks, strong accountability, and enforceable conflict-of-interest rules to ensure effective governance. The state must now ensure that commercial discipline, transparency and accountability guide its implementation.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Chromebook scheme
articles.content: THE government’s plan to distribute 500,000 Chromebooks to students over two years could help narrow Pakistan’s digital divide. The devices, which will come with MiFi internet connectivity, are meant for students handpicked under the scheme. In a country where access to computers and reliable internet still depends heavily on family income and location, that matters. A student who cannot afford a laptop should not be locked out of online learning, digital skills or job opportunities. But the value of the scheme will depend on how it is carried out. The state should publish clear eligibility criteria, ensure that poorer students are not crowded out by those who already have devices, and explain how the refurbished Chromebooks will be procured, tested and distributed. The total cost should also be disclosed, along with safeguards against political influence in selecting recipients and suppliers. There should also be a plan for repairs, replacement and technical support. A device that stops working after a few months, or cannot connect reliably outside major cities, will do little to close the gap it was meant to address. More importantly, access to hardware is only one part of Pakistan’s education problem. A Chromebook cannot compensate for weak teaching, poor literacy, overcrowded classrooms or schools without dependable electricity and internet access. Nor will handing out devices automatically improve learning. Teachers need training to use digital tools well, students need access to useful content, and schools need systems that can blend technology with ordinary classroom instruction. The government should therefore set measurable goals for the scheme: whether students use the devices regularly for learning, whether their digital skills improve, and whether this leads to better educational outcomes. Independent evaluation would help determine if the programme deserves expansion. There is also a case for giving students in remote and low-income areas greater weight, since they stand to benefit most from access they currently lack. Pakistan has launched laptop schemes before; what matters now is whether this one produces more than a distribution ceremony. Technology can widen opportunity, but only when it is tied to good teaching, reliable connectivity and clear educational purpose.
